article.title: Blue waves
article.author: Sirantos Fotopoulos
article.content: M illions of Americans delivered a well-deserved rebuke to Trump on Election Day, but the Democratic Party would be wise to resist the temptation to mistake an electorate’s hatred of Republican authoritarianism for an endorsement of corporate liberalism. The working class has spent forty years watching Democratic administrations convert blue waves into fresh mandates for the same economic establishment, and the historical record suggests that the only people likely to celebrate this victory without apprehension are the lobbyists, corporate donors, and political undertakers who have made a lucrative career out of burying popular expectations. The balance sheet on the last few blue waves The historical record is especially instructive because the U.S. has experienced several Democratic blue waves in recent decades, each accompanied by predictions of a new political settlement. In 1992, Bill Clinton arrived promising a different Democratic politics, supposedly capable of combining economic opportunity with social responsibility. What followed included the North American Free Trade Agreement, signed in 1993, and the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, which dismantled the existing federal welfare entitlement and replaced it with Temporary Assistance for Needy Families. Clinton subsequently signed legislation that imposed time limits and work requirements on assistance to poor families. The administration that had promised to make government work for ordinary Americans demonstrated considerable enthusiasm for making ordinary Americans accommodate the requirements of the market. The phrase “ending welfare as we know it” became an especially revealing description of the achievement. For working families, the consequences were considerably less amusing than the political marketing. Then came the Democratic victory of 2006, when widespread opposition to the Iraq War, Republican corruption, and the W. Bush administration’s economic policies delivered control of Congress to the Democrats. Nancy Pelosi became the first woman Speaker of the House, and the party promised a new direction for the country. Yet the political energy that had helped produce the victory was rapidly absorbed into the familiar routines of congressional management. The Iraq War continued, the financial system approached catastrophe, and the Democratic leadership demonstrated considerably more interest in restoring confidence among financial markets than in reorganizing the economic relationships that had produced the crisis. The wave had changed the occupants of congressional offices. It had yet to change the balance of power between capital and labor. The election of Barack Obama in 2008 produced perhaps the greatest expectations of any Democratic victory in modern American history. Millions believed that the 2008 financial catastrophe had finally discredited the economic establishment, that Wall Street would be forced to account for its conduct, and that working people would receive something resembling a New Deal for the twenty-first century. Obama inherited an extraordinary opportunity. His administration subsequently presided over the rescue and restructuring of the automobile industry, but the arrangement imposed substantial sacrifices on workers and retirees while preserving the corporate ownership structures that had helped produce the disaster. Shareholders and creditors absorbed losses, certainly, but autoworkers also faced plant closures, reduced employment, and the transfer of retiree healthcare obligations into a separate trust. The Employee Free Choice Act, which might have strengthened union organizing, died in Congress. Meanwhile, the financial system recovered with considerable assistance from public resources, while millions of households endured foreclosure, unemployment, and prolonged economic insecurity. The country received a historic president, Wall Street received a functioning rescue operation, and the working class was encouraged to regard recovery in the stock market as evidence of its own good fortune. The working class has spent forty years watching Democratic administrations convert blue waves into fresh mandates for the same economic establishment. The 2018 blue wave provides another useful exhibit. Democrats won 41 additional House seats, regained control of the chamber, and acquired a powerful institutional platform from which to challenge Trump’s administration. The result was politically important, and the subsequent investigations exposed serious abuses of presidential power. Yet the electoral victory produced little corresponding transformation in the economic organization of American society. Health care remained dominated by private insurers, labor protections remained inadequate, wealth concentration continued, and the basic relationship between corporate power and government survived largely intact. The Democratic leadership became increasingly adept at presenting the defense of constitutional institutions as a sufficient political program, even as millions of working people continued confronting stagnant wages, unaffordable housing, medical insecurity, and declining labor bargaining power. The 2020 Democratic victories were supposed to provide an especially decisive opportunity. Democrats controlled the presidency, the House, and the Senate, albeit with an exceptionally narrow Senate majority. There was a popular mandate for economic relief, and considerable public support for policies that would have materially improved working-class life. The $15 federal minimum wage proposal failed to survive the Senate’s procedural machinery. The PRO Act, which would have strengthened collective bargaining and workers’ organizing rights, failed to become law. The expanded Child Tax Credit, which had significantly reduced child poverty, expired after Congress declined to extend it. These were among the clearest illustrations of the distance between Democratic campaign promises and the actual distribution of political power within the party. The administration could accomplish important things, including substantial pandemic relief and infrastructure investment, but the interests of corporate America remained remarkably well represented throughout the process. A party capable of finding enormous resources when financial stability is threatened somehow discovers a more complicated set of constitutional and procedural difficulties when working people demand a larger share of national wealth. One might reasonably ask how many repetitions of this performance are required before the audience recognizes the production. The Democratic Party is a coalition, certainly, but its institutional leadership, major fundraising networks, and relationships with corporate America place formidable limits on its willingness to confront the ownership class. The party’s internal machinery remains deeply dependent upon wealthy donors, corporate fundraising, and the financial interests that dominate American politics. There are exceptions, insurgencies, and genuine reformers within its ranks. Yet the presence of progressive candidates on a Democratic ballot should never be confused with the political character of the institution they are attempting to change. Mass struggle, bourgeois parties, and the state The underlying question concerns the character of the state itself. In a capitalist society, government operates within an economic order whose commanding institutions remain overwhelmingly controlled by private owners. This gives capital enormous structural advantages, including the ability to influence economic conditions upon which elected governments depend. Yet the state is also a terrain of political struggle, and the history of labor movements demonstrates that organized people can force governments and employers to concede ground. The New Deal, the civil rights movement, the labor struggles of the twentieth century, and the expansion of social protections were achieved through combinations of political mass mobilization, economic disruption, and sustained popular pressure which at times included violent riots. The lesson is considerably more interesting than the parliamentary procedural romanticism of the Democratic establishment. A tenant union that prevents an eviction has altered the immediate balance of power between a landlord and a family. Workers who organize a credible strike have established a capacity to interrupt production and impose costs upon an employer. A neighborhood organization that mobilizes legal assistance, public solidarity, and material support against deportation has created a practical obstacle to the machinery of state coercion. These organizations possess something that campaign advertisements and congressional press conferences cannot manufacture: the capacity to make powerful interests confront consequences. Their achievements may eventually require legislation, but their initial strength comes from people acting collectively rather than waiting for permission from political representatives. The ballot can help create favorable conditions for such organization. It cannot substitute for it. The Democratic leadership will undoubtedly describe election 2026 as a historic mandate. The corporate donors will congratulate the party on its impressive performance. The television networks will discover a new collection of political personalities, and Washington will begin its elaborate ritual of interpreting electoral arithmetic as a substitute for social analysis. Meanwhile, the people who voted against Trump will return to work, pay their rent, confront their medical bills, worry about their children’s futures, and discover whether their political victory has improved the material conditions of their lives. They should demand evidence rather than expressions of gratitude. They should measure the incoming majority by wages raised, unions strengthened, housing made affordable, public services expanded, detention budgets challenged, and corporate privileges withdrawn. Another new blue wave can also become another episode in the long history of American electoral disappointment, where popular anger is converted into institutional legitimacy and the people who supplied the votes are subsequently invited to admire the wisdom of their representatives. The difference will be determined by what happens after the election, when the cameras depart and the lobbyists return to their offices. The working class has already supplied the votes. The incoming majority now has an opportunity to demonstrate what those votes were worth. But the decisive question belongs to the people themselves: whether they intend to remain an electoral constituency periodically summoned to rescue the Democratic Party from the abyss, or become an organized political force capable of making the entire political establishment answer to them. Four chances for the Democrats to disappoint The historical record explains where the party has failed before, and the coming years supply the occasions on which it may fail again, with consequences that reach well beyond the next set of primaries. The danger lies less in Democratic incompetence than in Democratic competence, because the party is extraordinarily skilled at the task its donors require of it, which is to stabilize the existing order at the moment that order is threatened. Each stabilization leaves a payment still due, the outstanding bill lands on the people who voted for the Democrats, and the demagogues of the next cycle are generous in their willingness to read the invoice aloud. Consider the artificial intelligence boom, which has become the largest debt-financed building campaign in modern corporate history. The five largest firms will have spent roughly $800 billion on capital projects in 2026 and are expected to approach $1.1 trillion in 2027, while borrowing for the buildout now accounts for around 30 percent of net investment-grade bond issuance Pension funds and insurers hold much of the paper. If revenue fails to arrive on schedule, the losses will be shifted to retirement savings and municipal budgets, and that route determines what any bailout rescue will be called. The party that controls both chambers will then face a choice its history has already answered. Leadership will describe the bailout as protection for pensioners, workers, and the municipalities that borrowed against promised data center revenue, and the description will carry a measure of truth, because the exposure is genuine. Yet the guarantee will flow to the executives, bondholders, and lenders who designed the structure, and it will arrive without equity stakes, without limits on compensation, without the breakup of any monopoly, and without a single protection for the households that lose their jobs or their homes while the markets recover. The sequence repeats 2008 with the labels changed, and the party that performs it will have spent public credit to preserve private ownership in the very industry whose lobbyists helped finance its campaigns. The Musks, Zuckerbergs, and Bezoses were once aligned with the Nancy Pelosi and Kamala Harris class before they swung their pendulum towards Trump. They will now swing towards the new Democratic Congressional leadership. It is in their interest to do so. No parasite can survive without a host. And, when the host dies, a new host must be pursued. The billionaire who has spent a career protecting his own fortune will campaign as the enemy of billionaires, and the evidence will be supplied by the Democratic leadership itself. No party survives in office whose voters are failed repeatedly while being told that the cure for failure is a larger turnout. The affordability crisis offers a second occasion for the party to disappoint its voters. The war with Iran, launched in late February without a declaration of Congress, has pushed crude oil above $100 a barrel, raised the costs of farming, trucking, and heating, and could add roughly half a percentage point to inflation in the first quarter of 2027, according to a Congressional Budget Office estimate. The House has passed a war powers resolution 3 times, and the Senate has voted on such a measure 14 times without ending the war, so the legislative record already shows what a resolution accomplishes against a president who vetoes it and a chamber that lacks the two-thirds majority required to override him. Democratic leaders will therefore hold a majority, a war, and a price level, with only one instrument capable of changing the first two, which is the power over appropriations. They will decline to use it, because every strategist in the party will warn that limits on war funding invite the charge of abandoning the troops and defying AIPAC, and the same strategists will advise against anything that hands the Right a slogan for 2028. Prices will remain high, and voters who have just been told that Democrats will come to the rescue will feel abandoned yet again. The most dangerous feature of the coming cycle is that the Right’s indictment [of the Democrats] will contain accurate claims. A third occasion arises in the budget itself. Appropriations bills carry the funding for detention, deportation, and military procurement alongside the funding for schools and hospitals, and leadership has a long habit of accepting the former in exchange for the latter. Hearings will expose abuses, officials will snub subpoenas, and the spending lines will be renewed anyway on the argument that a government shutdown would punish the vulnerable. The same vote that finances the machinery will be cited, correctly, by every organizer who is asked why the people who knocked on doors for the majority should knock again in 2028. A fourth chance for the Democrats to disappoint its voters lies in the politics of electricity and shelter. State legislatures controlled by Democrats will compete to attract data centers with tax abatements and discounted power contracts, and the households in those states will face higher utility bills, while the promised jobs prove to be a few hundred technicians at each site. Meanwhile the federal bills that would raise wages and strengthen unions will die behind the filibuster, as they did five years ago, and leadership will blame procedural obstacles—with sorrow and regret. Taken together, these occasions explain how the pendulum swings. No party survives in office whose voters are failed repeatedly while being told that the cure for failure is a larger turnout. The voters who supplied the majority will conclude, with considerable justification, that elections change the faces administering their circumstances and leave the circumstances intact. Some will withdraw into private exhaustion, while others, a crucial minority, will turn toward whichever movement offers an explanation for their suffering, and the authoritarian Right has never lacked explanations, since its explanations demand neither evidence nor accountability. A movement of the discarded must be organized by the discarded themselves, or it will be organized against them. The most dangerous feature of the coming cycle is that the Right’s indictment will contain accurate claims. Every claim that Democrats rescued the powerful, prolonged the costs of the war, and funded the ICE machinery they condemned will be demonstrable from the congressional record, and the demagogue who delivers those claims will pair them with an invented culprit, because a true grievance married to a false enemy is the oldest instrument in the authoritarian repertoire. A movement of the discarded must be organized by the discarded themselves, or it will be organized against them. Trump was defeated by a country that remembered what it had been promised and discovered it was still capable of collective refusal. That memory is now the most valuable and most perishable resource in American politics, and the Democratic Party holds it in trust with no evident intention of spending it on the people who deposited it. If the majority uses the memory to rescue the financiers of the next decade, to administer the costs of a war it declined to stop, and to fund the machinery it promised to investigate, then the country will learn in 2028 that the hand raised against the old authoritarianism can be raised for a new form of rule. The wave will have delivered what the owners wanted all along, which is a pause, and the pause will have been purchased with the patience of everyone who believed it was a beginning. Only an organized people can make it a beginning, and the hour for organizing arrives while the wave still stands, before the water finds its level. The Democrats are riding into office on a wave of popular revolt against tyranny, but the party will take every chance to disappoint—unless the struggle is organized to continue.
